files.made: F.W. Murnau, for Prana Film, Berlin
files.means: The only film the studio ever made
files.lost: Prana Film was founded in 1921 by a businessman and an occultist painter to make films about the supernatural. It made exactly one. Nosferatu was Dracula with the names filed off, and its own premiere programme admitted it was "freely adapted" from Bram Stoker's novel. That is how Stoker's widow, Florence, found out. She sued and won. By then Prana was bankrupt and could not pay her a pfennig, so in July 1925 a German court did the only thing left: it ordered every negative and every print destroyed.
files.found: The film had already left the building. Prints were playing in Budapest and Paris by 1922, a copy reached the London Film Society in 1925, and it opened in New York in 1929. No one has ever found evidence that a single print was burned. A company that made one film lost it in court, and the film outlived the company, the verdict and the widow.
files.fact: Count Orlok's castle is real: Orava Castle, in what is now northern Slovakia.

files.cause: Lost its name, and its notice
files.made: George A. Romero, for Image Ten, near Evans City, Pennsylvania
files.means: About $114,000, raised $600 at a time
files.lost: A Pittsburgh company that made commercials and industrial films raised the money from ten backers, $600 each to start, and cast its own clients and neighbours as the dead. The blood was Bosco chocolate syrup; the flesh was ham from a local butcher. The film was called Night of the Flesh Eaters until the distributor changed the title. The notice of ownership sat on the old title card, and it did not make the trip to the new prints. Under the law of the day, a film released without a notice had none.
files.found: It opened at the Fulton Theater in downtown Pittsburgh on 1 October 1968 and never stopped playing. Because anyone could print it, everyone did: hundreds of unauthorised tapes, discs and late-night broadcasts carried it into every house in America. The film that invented the modern zombie spread exactly the way its zombies do. It entered the National Film Registry in 1999.
files.fact: Romero didn't forget the notice. It was lost when someone else renamed his film.

files.made: Herk Harvey, a maker of classroom films from Lawrence, Kansas
files.means: $33,000 and about three weeks
files.lost: Herk Harvey spent his working life making industrial and educational films at Centron in Lawrence, Kansas. On a drive home from California he passed the ruins of the Saltair Pavilion on the Great Salt Lake, and decided to make one feature before he died. The Salt Lake Chamber of Commerce rented him the place for a week for $50. His crew was five people. His distributor cut nine minutes to fit a double bill, the film flopped, Harvey's royalty cheque bounced, and the distributor was gone by 1964.
files.found: Late-night television kept it alive for thirty years, playing to insomniacs who had no idea who made it. Around 1989 it came back to theatres, and the audience that had been haunted by it for decades finally met it properly. Harvey lived to see the revival and died in 1996. It is still his only feature, and he is in it: he plays The Man.
files.fact: Candace Hilligoss was the only trained actor in the cast. She was paid about $2,000.

files.made: Ida Lupino, for The Filmakers, released by RKO
files.means: Around $100,000, shot in the Alabama Hills near Lone Pine
files.lost: In 1952 Ida Lupino was the only woman directing in Hollywood, working out of the small company she ran with Collier Young. She went to San Quentin to meet Billy Cook, a real killer who had held men hostage on a desert road, and bought the rights to his story. Cook was executed that December, before the film came out, and the censors made her rename him. The Filmakers lasted five years. When it closed, nobody was left to look after its films.
files.found: For decades The Hitch-Hiker circulated in murky copies, filed with the cheap B-noirs. Then the reputation turned: it entered the National Film Registry in 1998, a restored 35mm print premiered in 2014, and it is now held up as a classic American noir directed by a woman. Seventy-one minutes, three men in a car, and nowhere to hide.
files.fact: Lupino wasn't Hollywood's first woman director. Dorothy Arzner came before her. In 1952 she was the only one.

files.cause: Poverty Row; nobody kept a good copy
files.made: Edgar G. Ulmer, for Producers Releasing Corporation (PRC)
files.means: Fourteen camera days, June 1945
files.lost: PRC was the bottom of Poverty Row, a studio that turned out programmers to fill the lower half of a double bill. Detour was one of them: a hitchhiker, a stranger's dead body, and a woman who knows too much. It was made fast and treated as disposable, and for fifty years that is how it was seen: in washed-out copies of copies, the only way anyone could watch it. The legend says it was shot in six days for $20,000. The shooting script says fourteen, and the real cost was closer to $100,000.
files.found: A preservationist spent about ten years looking for a good print. She found one at the Cinémathèque royale in Brussels, struck from the camera negative, with French and Flemish subtitles burned into every frame. They were painted out by hand, frame by frame. The restoration premiered in 2018. A film nobody had kept was finally seen as it was shot.
files.fact: The "six days, $20,000" legend began with Ulmer himself, in a 1972 interview.

files.made: Stanley Kubrick, age 24, with money from his uncle's pharmacy
files.means: Fourteen people in the San Gabriel Mountains
files.lost: The whole company was five actors, five crew including Kubrick's wife, and three labourers to carry equipment up the mountain. It is a war film about four soldiers trapped behind enemy lines in no particular war. It premiered at Venice in 1952, and Kubrick spent the rest of his life trying to make it disappear. When a New York cinema announced a screening in 1994, his studio put out a statement calling it "a bumbling amateur film exercise."
files.found: The screening went ahead. The story that Kubrick destroyed the negative has never been proven. Later, the Library of Congress found a 35mm element of the original 70-minute cut, the version Venice saw before Kubrick trimmed it, and it came back to cinemas in 2023. It is the one Kubrick film he tried to un-make. It is also the only place to see him start.
files.fact: Private Sidney is played by a young Paul Mazursky, who became a director himself.

files.made: Herbert J. Biberman, Michael Wilson and Paul Jarrico, all blacklisted
files.means: About $250,000, partly from a miners' union
files.lost: Three men Hollywood had banished for their politics went to Silver City, New Mexico, to film the true story of a zinc miners' strike, with the strikers playing themselves. Film labs were told not to process it. Projectionists were told not to show it. Mid-shoot, the lead actress, Rosaura Revueltas, was arrested and deported to Mexico. She recorded her last lines in secret, across the border.
files.found: It was never banned. It was boycotted so thoroughly it didn't need to be: a dozen theatres showed it, and then it disappeared for a decade. It came back through union halls, college campuses and film societies, and became a founding film of the Chicano movement. In 1992 it entered the National Film Registry, the list of films the country has decided to keep.
files.fact: Juan Chacón, the male lead, was the real president of the union local. It was his only film.

files.made: Howard Hawks, for Columbia Pictures
files.means: Seven days over schedule, autumn 1939
files.lost: Hawks took The Front Page, a play about two newspapermen, and made one of them a woman. That made it one of the fastest-talking pictures Hollywood ever made: about 240 words a minute, against roughly 90 in the average film of the day. A studio's hold on a film then lasted 28 years, and keeping it meant filing again. At the end of the 1960s, for His Girl Friday, nobody filed. One of the best comedies ever made slipped out of the studio's hands over a form.
files.found: It went everywhere: budget video labels, television, school libraries, the dollar bin. It was the definitive screwball comedy, and it was available to anyone. It entered the National Film Registry in 1993. A lot of people who love this film first saw it for almost nothing.
files.fact: Cary Grant ad-libbed a joke about Archie Leach, his own birth name.

files.cause: Written day by day, re-cut, and let go
files.made: John Huston, on the Amalfi Coast, with Humphrey Bogart's own money
files.means: Bogart's company, Santana, put its own cash in
files.lost: The script wasn't finished when shooting began in Ravello, so Truman Capote wrote it on the spot, two or three days ahead of the cameras. He and Huston decided to play the whole thing as a joke. On the way to one location Bogart was in a car crash that cost him his front-teeth bridge. Preview audiences were baffled, the producers re-cut it into a flashback with a new Bogart voiceover, and it lost money, including Bogart's.
files.found: The film Bogart dismissed as one "only phonies like" found the people who liked it: a cult of fans who worked out it was a parody all along. In 2016 an uncut international version turned up in a London vault. It was restored without the voiceover and with four lost minutes back in, closer to what Huston and Capote meant.
files.fact: Capote wrote pages two or three days ahead of the cameras, in the hotel, as they went.

files.cause: Its own star's company let it lapse
files.made: Andrew V. McLaglen, for John Wayne's Batjac
files.means: Old Tucson Studios and the Arizona borderlands
files.lost: McLintock! was a family business: John Wayne's company produced it, his son Michael produced it, and his son Patrick is in it. It was a hit. Then, in 1991, when its first term ran out, nobody filed the papers to keep it. Within two years, tapes of it were in the shops.
files.found: The Wayne family sued in 1996 to win it back. They argued that the unpublished script drafts were still protected, and in 1998 a federal appeals court ruled against them. Few films have a court ruling in their history quite like it. The family's company later released restored editions of the film their own company had let go.
files.fact: The music was treated separately: the score stayed protected after the picture lapsed.

files.cause: The maker saw nothing from it
files.made: Tom Graeff, who did almost every job himself
files.means: About $14,000, shot around Hollywood
files.lost: Tom Graeff produced, wrote, directed, shot and edited it, did the effects, and acted in it under another name. One investor put in $5,000 in exchange for playing the villain. The monster was the shadow of a small animal, magnified, because a real one was beyond the budget. Warner Bros. bought it, renamed it, and put it on the bottom half of a drive-in double bill. Graeff and his backers never saw a return, and the film slipped out of their hands.
files.found: In 1992 Mystery Science Theater 3000 aired it to a national audience. Since then a biographer has spent years recovering Graeff's story, and his films are held at the UCLA Film & Television Archive. The film is sincere, strange, and made with more hope than money: a young man's whole ambition, left behind for anyone to find.
files.fact: The working title was The Boy From Out of This World. Warner chose the one on the poster.

files.cause: Held hostage by a lab bill
files.made: Curtis Harrington, for Virgo Productions, in Santa Monica
files.means: Eighteen days, summer 1960
files.lost: A sailor on shore leave falls for a woman who plays a mermaid in a pier sideshow and may believe it. It was Dennis Hopper's first leading role, and the occult artist Cameron played the sea witch. It premiered at the Spoleto festival in 1961 and then sat on a shelf, because the small company that made it couldn't pay its film lab. Roger Corman stepped in, and it finally opened in 1963. Nobody kept the papers up, and for years it survived only in poor copies.
files.found: The film's own material was in terrible shape. Some negative reels had warped into octagons, "like stop signs." Archivists at the Academy Film Archive restored it, and in 2020 Nicolas Winding Refn's company released a 4K restoration. A mermaid movie from the Santa Monica pier finally has a proper print.
files.fact: It took until January 1966 to reach a cinema in Los Angeles, a few miles from where it was shot.

files.cause: Never registered; made to be forgotten
files.made: Roger Corman, for The Filmgroup
files.means: About $30,000 and sets already standing
files.lost: Corman expected nothing from it after its first run and never registered it. The legend says he shot it in two days to win a bet. The people who were there say there was no bet. The interiors were shot in two days and a night after three days of rehearsal, and the street scenes were grabbed later on four evenings by a non-union crew. The lead actor was paid $400 for the week.
files.found: Local television played it for twenty years, a flesh-eating plant turning up between the weather and the late movie, until a 1982 stage musical made it famous all over again. The cheapest film Corman ever made became the one his name is most often attached to.
files.fact: The dental patient who enjoys the drill is a very young Jack Nicholson, and he improvised most of it.

files.made: Roger Corman, for AIP
files.means: $50,000 and five days
files.lost: A busboy at a beatnik café accidentally kills a cat, covers it in clay, and is hailed as a genius. He then needs more subjects. Corman called it an affectionate satire on a scene that was about to be swept away by the hippies, and he made it on sets left over from another picture. When its papers came due, nobody filed them.
files.found: Dick Miller, who plays Walter Paisley, the busboy turned sculptor, got his only real lead out of it and never forgot him. For the next thirty years he kept playing characters named Walter Paisley, in The Howling, Twilight Zone: The Movie and more, a private joke carried from film to film. The busboy outlived his own movie.
files.fact: The Little Shop of Horrors was shot soon afterwards, on the same sets.

files.made: Joseph H. Lewis, for Security Pictures and Theodora Productions
files.means: Twenty-six days; United Artists pulled out
files.lost: The backer walked away before the start, so the producers took it to a smaller distributor. Jack Palance quit the day before shooting; Richard Conte read the script that afternoon and started the next morning. It was planned in colour and shot in black and white to save money, which may be the luckiest saving in noir. The New York Times called it shrill and old-fashioned. Reportedly, its paperwork was never properly filed.
files.found: What the critics dismissed, cinematographers studied. John Alton lit it with almost nothing: single sources, fog, and faces cut out of the dark. The film became a textbook of how to shoot noir. It was restored in HD in 2018, and a 4K edition is on the way for its seventieth anniversary.
files.fact: The two hitmen are written as a couple, which was unusually open for 1955.

files.made: Rudolph Maté, for the Popkin brothers' Cardinal Pictures
files.means: Shot on the streets of San Francisco and Los Angeles
files.lost: A man walks into a police station to report a murder: his own. He has been poisoned, and he has a day or two to find out who did it. The short-lived company that made it is long gone, and when its papers came due, a filing error meant they weren't done in time. The film with the best premise in noir was left with nobody to claim it.
files.found: Cheap copies kept it circulating for decades, and it was remade four times, in 1969, 1988, 2017 and 2022. In 2004 the Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry. Edmond O'Brien's run down Market Street was shot without a permit, and the passers-by who stop to stare are real.
files.fact: Rudolph Maté shot The Passion of Joan of Arc before he ever directed.

files.made: Orson Welles, for producer Sam Spiegel
files.means: $1,034,000, on time and under budget
files.lost: Welles, needing to prove he could be trusted, took a thriller about a war criminal hiding as a teacher in a Connecticut town. His contract let the producers take the film away from him. The editor cut thirty-two pages of script, including a Latin American chase that is now thought to be lost. It was the only Welles film to make a profit on first release, and in 1973 the producers let it go.
files.found: For decades it survived in bad copies. The Library of Congress kept a 35mm print, and an HD release was made from it in 2013. Archivists in Paris and Washington are now restoring it from the original negatives. Edward G. Robinson hunts Welles through the town, and the story earned an Oscar nomination.
files.fact: Welles said a scar he got on this set always reminded him of what was cut from the film.

files.made: Stanley Donen, for Arthur Freed at MGM
files.means: About $1.6 million, summer 1950
files.lost: It went through two leading ladies before shooting began: June Allyson became pregnant, and Judy Garland was suspended. Fred Astaire's own life was in the story: his sister and dance partner, Adele, had left the act to marry an English lord. In the late 1970s the richest studio in Hollywood let the paperwork lapse on a handful of its early-fifties films. Royal Wedding was one of them.
files.found: Freed from the studio, it went everywhere, and so did its best scene. Astaire dances up the walls and across the ceiling of a hotel room, in a set built inside a rotating drum with the camera bolted to it. That clip became one of the most copied moments in film. The whole film came with it, for anyone.
files.fact: Winston Churchill's daughter Sarah plays Astaire's love interest, her first American film.

files.cause: Two brothers, eleven days, borrowed sets
files.made: Victor and Edward Halperin, independents, released by United Artists
files.means: About $50,000 and eleven days in March 1932
files.lost: Two brothers with no studio of their own made the first feature-length zombie film on other people's leftovers. They rented the great hall from Dracula, the corridors from Frankenstein, and a balcony from the 1923 Hunchback of Notre Dame, and they shot at night because days cost more. Bela Lugosi, a year after Dracula, played a Haitian mill owner who works the dead in his fields. The longer cut shown at the New York premiere has never been found. What survives came down through decades of reissues and quarrels over who controlled the originals.
files.found: The legend says it was lost until the 1960s. It wasn't: it was reissued in 1951. What it lost was its standing, and it got that back slowly, as the film every zombie picture after it quietly descends from. There is still no fully satisfying restoration, and the original negative's whereabouts remain part of the mystery.
files.fact: The dead mill workers were the first zombies a feature film ever showed.

files.cause: A company that made one film
files.made: Phil Karlson, for Associated Players and Producers, released by United Artists
files.means: Samuel Goldwyn Studios, with Catalina Island playing Mexico
files.lost: Edward Small and two partners set up a company to make thirteen pictures. They made one, then dissolved it. It's a heist film in which the gang wear masks so that none of them can identify the others. The ex-con framed for their robbery goes to a Mexican resort to find them one by one, knowing none of their faces. Nobody was left to file the papers when its first term ran out, and for years it circulated in shabby copies.
files.found: Its idea didn't need a good print to travel. Masked strangers, a split, and nobody trusting anybody: Quentin Tarantino has named it an influence on Reservoir Dogs. The studio holding the original elements finally issued a proper edition in 2007, and a new restoration followed. A company that never made its second film made one that's still borrowed from.
files.fact: Its working title was Kansas City 117, after a police radio code.

files.made: Fritz Lang, for Diana Productions, released by Universal
files.means: $1.2 million; the first film of Lang's own company
files.lost: Fritz Lang, Joan Bennett and producer Walter Wanger formed a company of their own, and this was its first picture. Edward G. Robinson plays a meek cashier and Sunday painter who is ruined by a con woman and her lover. New York State's censors banned it outright, then Milwaukee and Atlanta, whose censor called it "licentious, profane, obscure." It was cut before it could play; one stabbing went from seven blows to one. The company collapsed two films later. Nobody kept its papers up.
files.found: The film the censors fought now sits among Lang's best work. It was restored from a Library of Congress print and later from a 4K scan of a nitrate fine grain, and it is still one of the bleakest endings Hollywood allowed in the forties.
files.fact: The paintings credited to Robinson's character are real, by the artist John Decker.

files.made: Joseph Green and Rex Carlton, independents, around Tarrytown, New York
files.means: About $62,000, as The Black Door
files.lost: A surgeon keeps his fiancée's severed head alive in a tray in his lab while he goes out looking for a new body for it. Finished in 1959, it sat on a shelf for three years; accounts differ on whether it was too lurid to sell or its makers ran out of money. When AIP finally released it in 1962, cut down, the notice on the prints was reportedly defective. It went out into the world with nobody holding it.
files.found: In 1993 Mystery Science Theater 3000 made it the first film Mike Nelson watched as host, and a generation met it that way. Uncut versions later restored more of what 1962 had removed.
files.fact: The creature in the closet was Eddie Carmel, later photographed by Diane Arbus as "the Jewish Giant."

files.cause: Made for a tax break; its company folded
files.made: Roger Corman, for The Filmgroup, in Puerto Rico
files.means: About a week, in colour, back to back with two other films
files.lost: Corman learned there were tax incentives for anything "manufactured" in Puerto Rico, and decided that included movies. He shot three back to back. This one had no finished script, so its writer, Robert Towne, already paid, was cast as the third lead to keep him on hand, under a false name. Towne later said the film confirmed he wasn't an actor. The Filmgroup, which Corman founded with his brother, closed in 1968, and its films were largely left unprotected.
files.found: Three survivors of the end of the world, on an empty island paradise, bickering. It's remembered now as the first produced screenplay by the man who went on to write Chinatown. It first played on a double bill with The Little Shop of Horrors, File No. 013.
files.fact: Creature from the Haunted Sea was shot on the same trip, with the same cast, partly on film left over from this one.

files.made: Ubaldo Ragona and Sidney Salkow, a US-Italian co-production shot in Rome
files.means: Black and white, to save money; Rome's EUR district as an American town
files.lost: Hammer Films bought Richard Matheson's novel I Am Legend and had him adapt it, until British censors warned the script would be banned as written. Hammer sold it on, and it was shot in Rome with Vincent Price as the last man alive, hunting by day the things that hunt him by night. Matheson hated the rewrite so much that he put a pen name on it, Logan Swanson. The book's own author refused his name, and its rights drifted with it.
files.found: Four years later, a Pittsburgh commercials company made Night of the Living Dead, File No. 002, and George Romero said plainly where the idea came from: I Am Legend. The man the book's author disowned became the ancestor of every siege by the dead that followed.
files.fact: Matheson said he'd have preferred Jack Palance to Vincent Price.
